parts.prompt: Find \( f'(x) \). Find all values of \( x \) at which \( f'(x) = 0 \) or \( f'(x) \) is undefined.
parts.answer_latex: f'(x) = 0 \text{ at } x = 0, \ x = 2; \ \text{undefined at } x = 1

worked_solution.text: The numerator factors as x times (x - 2); the denominator is zero at x = 1.

points.criterion: Applies the quotient rule and gives f'(x) = (x^2 - 2x)/(x - 1)^2 or an equivalent form, such as 1 - 1/(x - 1)^2.
Gives f'(x) = 0 at x = 0 and x = 2, and f'(x) undefined at x = 1, from the factored numerator and the denominator.

parts.prompt: Find all open intervals on which \( f \) is increasing. Give a reason for your answer.

worked_solution.text: The denominator is positive for x not 1, so f' has the sign of x(x - 2).

points.criterion: Gives the interval x < 0, that is (-infinity, 0), with or without its endpoint.
Gives the interval x > 2, that is (2, infinity), with or without its endpoint.
States that f'(x) > 0 on these intervals. A bare sign chart with no statement naming f' does not earn the point.

parts.prompt: Find all open intervals on which \( f \) is decreasing. Give a reason for your answer.

worked_solution.text: For 0 < x < 2 the numerator x(x - 2) is negative; x = 1 is not in the domain, so the interval splits there.
worked_solution.latex: f'(x) < 0 \text{ on } 0 < x < 1 \text{ and on } 1 < x < 2

points.criterion: Gives the two intervals 0 < x < 1 and 1 < x < 2, with or without the endpoints 0 and 2. The single interval 0 < x < 2, which crosses x = 1 where f is undefined, does not earn the point.
States that f'(x) < 0 on these intervals.

parts.prompt: Find the absolute minimum value of \( f \) on the interval \( x > 1 \). Justify your answer.

worked_solution.text: On x > 1 the only critical point is x = 2, where f' changes from negative to positive.
worked_solution.latex: f'(x) < 0 \text{ on } 1 < x < 2, \quad f'(x) > 0 \text{ on } x > 2

worked_solution.text: So f decreases to x = 2 and increases after it, and f(2) is the least value on the whole interval.

points.criterion: States that f' < 0 on 1 < x < 2 and f' > 0 for x > 2, and that x = 2 is the only critical point on x > 1, so f has its absolute minimum on that interval at x = 2. A local first or second derivative test with no statement that x = 2 is the only critical point on the interval does not earn the point.
Gives the value f(2) = 4, found by substituting x = 2 into f.
